_work.title: Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn wa-al-jawhar al-maknūn (Princeton, Islamic Mss, 17c Arabic)
_work.blurb: A 17th-century Arabic manuscript at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett collection, gift 1942; figgy 1626111a), titled Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn wa-al-jawhar al-maknūn (The Hidden Secret and the Concealed Gem). The text is attributed to al-Ghazzālī but describes itself in the preface as 'an extract from the Kitāb al-Jafr of the Imam ʻAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib' — placing it squarely in the Shia divinatory tradition of the Jafr (jabr), the legendary book of esoteric knowledge attributed to the fourth caliph Ali and later to Imam Jafar al-Sadiq (6th Imam, d. 765 CE). The manuscript consists of 54 leaves of paper with red frame-ruling and covers a numbered series of magical operations (The Third Operation, The Fourteenth Operation, etc.), each presenting a complete praxis: divine names and Quranic verses to recite, talisman forms to draw, ritual timing, materials (oud, saffron, frankincense), and the specific wafq (magic square) or geometric diagram to inscribe. The manuscript contains three categories of visual content: (1) embedded numeric magic squares (wafq) associated with the angel Gabriel and Quranic names, labeled at the corners with angelic designations; (2) geometric talisman diagrams drawn in red and black ink — most notably an X-cross-within-square form (the 'Fourteenth Operation') in which two diagonal lines in red divide a square into four angular sections, each section containing a letter value; (3) divination tables in Ottoman-influenced later additions near the end of the manuscript, containing numbered grid cells with geomantic marks. The text includes first-person testimonial passages in which Imam Jafar al-Sadiq describes using a specific wafq on a sultan and achieving his desired outcome — a narrative device common in the Jafr tradition to validate the efficacy of each operation. Princeton University Library, Garrett collection, figgy UUID 1626111a.

entries.title: Jafr Magic Square — Numeric Wafq with Gabriel Label, Embedded in Text (f. 9a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, embedded numeric grid
entries.summary: Folio 9 recto of the Princeton Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn wa-al-jawhar al-maknūn (Garrett collection, 17c), containing a numeric magic square (wafq) embedded within the text of a red-bordered page. The wafq appears mid-page within the flowing Arabic text: a bordered rectangular grid of approximately 3×3 cells with Arabic numerals written in each cell, some highlighted in red ink. At the top right of the grid is the label 'جبرائل' (Jibrāʾīl — Gabriel), identifying this wafq as one of the angelic series associated with the four noble angels (ملائكة الكرام) of the Islamic Jafr tradition. The surrounding text discusses the operation's purpose — drawing together distant people and creating bonds between rulers and subjects — and specifies that the wafq should be written with 'the Ha' (the divine name element) in the middle cell along with the names of the seeker and the sought, then the four angelic names written at the four corners (الزوايا الأربع). The text explicitly references 'the Jafr' (الجفر) as the source of these 'mighty Quranic verses' ('ربع كلمات على أربع زوايا هذا الخاتم الكريم' — four words at the four corners of this noble seal), and mentions four noble angels (ملائكة الكرام) who manage contraction and expansion. The embedded-in-text format (rather than a dedicated diagram page) is characteristic of practical Jafr manuals where each operation includes its wafq form inline with the operational instructions.

entries.title: Red Diagonal-Cross Talisman — The Fourteenth Operation (f. 17a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink and red ink on paper, geometric talisman diagram
entries.summary: The most visually striking page of the Princeton Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn (Garrett collection, 17c), showing a geometric talisman diagram for the Fourteenth Operation ('العمل الرابع عشر', written in bold red calligraphy at center-left). The diagram consists of a large square drawn in black ink containing two diagonal lines drawn in vivid red ink, creating an X-cross that divides the square interior into four triangular sections. The label 'جبرائل' (Gabriel) appears at the top right of the diagram with additional annotation marks. Letter-number values are written in each of the four triangular sections created by the red diagonals: these are the corner values of the angelic square that define this talisman's magical properties. At the bottom of the diagram is a secondary drawn element — a smaller decorated shape below the main square. The text flanking the diagram specifies the complete operation: 'Here you write the complete wafq and the Quranic verses (الوفق بتمامه وآيات) and the Noble Angels (وملائكة الكرام) / and you write with the Ha' the name of the seeker and the name of the sought (اسم الطالب واسم المطلوب) / then the name of the night-star constellations (ثم اسم نوائل المنازل)'. The instruction continues with ritual materials: white silk cloth (خرقة حريرة ابيض), musk, saffron (زعفران), aloes wood (دمرهد), followed by 100 recitations of 'God is One' (قل هو الله أحد) and the Jafr verses (بالآيات الجفريات), 45 and then 35 times. The X-cross-within-square geometry is a specific talisman form in the Jafr/Sufi magical tradition, with each triangle encoding a divine attribute or angelic name.

entries.title: 5×5 Numeric Jafr Wafq — Imam Jafar Sultan-Court Efficacy Testimony (f. 26b)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, bordered numeric grid
entries.summary: A folio from the Princeton Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn (Garrett collection, 17c) combining a 5×5 numeric magic square (wafq) with one of the most vivid first-person testimonial passages in the Jafr manuscript tradition. The wafq occupies the lower left of the page: a bordered 5×5 grid (25 cells) with Arabic numerals filling each cell, one cell highlighted in red ink. The visible numbers include 1, 18, 10, 33 in the top row and descending values throughout — this is an abjad-derived wafq where the row, column, and diagonal sums encode the numerical value of a specific divine name. The abjad calculation notations below the grid (reading '٨٨٨٥' and other totals) confirm the computational basis: the scribe has verified that the cell sums correspond to the target abjad total. The annotation 'اللوح كما ترى' (The tablet as you see it) identifies this as a direct transcription of the talisman form from an authoritative source. To the right of the wafq, the headings 'كفاية فاعرفه واكتمه' (This is sufficient — know it and keep it secret) and 'صاراليك وهن صفة' (These qualities/descriptions have come to you) frame the revelation of a secret. The main text above contains the extraordinary testimonial: 'قال الإمام الجعفر رحمه الله وحق تربة جدي كتبته وعلقته على عضدي فادخلت به على سلطان وطلبت منه حاجتي فأقضاها وما تحدثت به على أحد من الأكابر وقصدت شيئاً إلا أبلغت مرادي الآمن خيرا وشراً وحلالا وحراماً' — 'Imam Jafar said, may God have mercy on him: By the soil of my grandfather, I wrote it and tied it to my arm and entered upon a sultan and asked for my need and he fulfilled it, and whenever I wanted something from the great ones I achieved my desire whether for good or evil, lawful or forbidden.' This narrative pattern — first-person testimonial by Imam Jafar al-Sadiq vouching for an operation's efficacy — is the defining rhetorical device of the Jafr tradition, linking each wafq to the imam's personal authority.

entries.title: Divinatory Grid with Geomantic Marks — Late MS Addition (f. 53a)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, drawn grid with geomantic notations
entries.summary: A late folio from the Princeton Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn (Garrett collection, 17c), folio 53 recto, written in a different hand than the main manuscript — a looser, more rapidly written script characteristic of Ottoman-influenced later additions or end-matter pages. The page is headed with 'بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم' (In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate) followed by the number '53' and a section title ('صح فحص' — Correct Examination/Verified Search). The main text body discusses a sequence of magical operations in Ottoman-influenced Arabic. In the lower left of the page, occupying approximately one quarter of the page area, is a hand-drawn divinatory grid: a rectangular table with 3–4 columns and 4–5 rows, created by drawing intersecting horizontal and vertical lines in ink. The cells of the grid contain Arabic numerals and small special marks — dots, short dashes, and curved symbols — that are characteristic of Islamic geomantic notation (ʻilm al-raml, divination by sand/dots). The marks include single dots, paired dots arranged vertically, and number-letter combinations. In the margins flanking the grid are additional notational elements — letter or number designations for each row or category. This drawn-in-hand grid differs from the neat ruled wafq squares of the earlier manuscript pages and appears to be a working divination table rather than a formal talisman, possibly added by a later owner or reader to record a specific divination inquiry. The presence of this informal divinatory notation in the back matter of the Sirr al-Masun reflects the manuscript's use as a practical working manual rather than a scholarly treatise.
